title: Quantum--classical break-even in electronic dynamics of macrocyclic molecules
authors: Shu Kanno, Kenji Sugisaki, Takashi Imamichi, Toshinari Itoko, Rei Sakuma, Hajime Nakamura, Qi Gao, Naoki Yamamoto
abstract: Here we demonstrate quantum--classical break-even for chemical dynamics applications, reaching useful accuracy with a quantum-hardware wall-clock time comparable to that estimated for practical classical computing resources. Specifically, we construct a quantum workflow for electronic dynamics based on tensor-network circuit compression leveraging spatial locality, extending circuit compression beyond one-dimensional open-boundary systems. This enables application of the workflow to problems that are hardware-native but classically hard. The workflow targets one-dimensional periodic Hamiltonians: circuits classically optimized only for short-time evolution within a small spatial region can be replicated in both space and time to construct long-time dynamics of the full system without classically simulating the corresponding large-scale evolution. We apply the workflow to cyclic conjugated macrocycles with rotational periodicity, 12-qubit benzene and 120-qubit [60]annulene, by embedding their electronic structure onto loops of IBM quantum processors. For the annulene, the quantum-processing-unit (QPU) wall-clock times for hole-doped nonequilibrium dynamics became comparable to the estimated wall-clock time of two classical methods, Majorana propagation and matrix-product-state time evolution based on the time-dependent variational principle; this corresponds to tens to hundreds of compute nodes depending on the task (36 CPU cores per node), assuming near-ideal parallel scaling, bringing the quantum calculation into a wall-clock-time regime comparable to conventional parallel high-performance-computing resources. We also show a situation in which a hybrid quantum--classical calculation is a reasonable choice in terms of both accuracy and computational time. These results show that quantum hardware can become a realistic computational option for chemically relevant electronic dynamics.
summary: This paper presents a quantum workflow to simulate electronic dynamics in large macrocycles, aiming to achieve 'quantum-classical break-even.' By using circuit compression based on spatial locality, the authors demonstrated that quantum processing times for systems like [60]annulene are becoming comparable to state-of-the-art classical supercomputing estimates, validating quantum hardware for molecular physics.
main_problem: Demonstrating quantum-classical break-even for simulating electronic dynamics in large macrocyclic molecules using quantum hardware.
main_result: The quantum workflow achieved wall-clock times for hole-doped dynamics in [60]annulene comparable to advanced classical methods, suggesting quantum hardware is a viable tool for chemical dynamics.
method: The authors developed a quantum workflow utilizing tensor-network circuit compression to construct long-time dynamics by replicating short-time evolution units across space and time.
model_or_system: The study focuses on electronic dynamics in macrocyclic molecules, specifically benzene (12-qubit) and [60]annulene (120-qubit), whose electronic structure is mapped onto loops of IBM quantum processors.
key_observables: One-body Pauli Z operators ($\langle Z_l angle$) and two-body Pauli Z operators ($\langle Z_l Z_m angle$) are measured to track non-equilibrium hole dynamics.
important_parameters: The comparison is made against classical methods like Majorana propagation and MPS time evolution, targeting a wall-clock time regime comparable to conventional HPC resources.
main_assumptions: The method relies on leveraging spatial locality via circuit compression and assumes that neglecting higher-order interaction terms is justified due to small spatial overlap.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the quantum workflow for cyclic molecules, detailing the steps of fractional system choice, local gate optimization, and space-time gate replication for the [60]annulene model.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the quantum workflow for dynamics, applies it to benzene and annulene, details the use of the Local Hilbert-Schmidt Test (LHST) for circuit optimization, and discusses the comparison of quantum time scales against state-of-the-art classical simulations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the computational bottleneck in simulating complex molecular electronic structure, providing a concrete pathway for quantum computation to tackle chemically relevant, time-dependent quantum dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the quantum workflow for dynamics of cyclic molecules. (a) [60]annulene (120-qubit) model and the mapped loop adopted in this study. (b) Workflow including the fractional system choice, local (translationally invariant) gate optimization, and space-time gate replication. This workflow constructs a quantum circuit to simulate a ring molecule by replicating a fundamental unit cell. This unit cell functions as a unitary gate designed to evolve the quantum state by a prescribed time step ∆t, and its repeated execution achieves time evolution of the total system under Htot for a total time t that is an integer multiple of ∆t.
Figure 2: The expectation value calculation for benzene. The error bar comes from a standard deviation for zero-noise extrapolations.
